title: Keeping money safe: the everyday basics
description: Most money is lost to tricks rather than break-ins — a few plain habits close the doors that tricksters rely on.

body.heading: Slow down at the moment of pressure
paragraphs: Scams about money almost always manufacture urgency: pay now, verify now, or lose everything. Real banks and tax offices do not demand instant payment by gift card or transfer, and they never ask for card details over the phone.
Pausing is a genuine security tool. Put the phone down, find the organisation's real number yourself, and ask. A legitimate caller will never mind you checking.

body.heading: Keys, codes, and passwords
paragraphs: Use a different password for banking than for shopping or social media, and turn on two-step verification wherever it is offered. The code sent to your phone is a second lock, and it stops most break-ins even if a password leaks.
Never share one-time codes. No genuine company asks you to read a code aloud or type it into a page reached from a link they sent you.

body.heading: Check the record often
paragraphs: Look through your transactions once a week. Small unfamiliar charges are worth querying immediately — criminals often test a stolen card with a tiny purchase first.
If something is wrong, contact your bank using the number on your card. Acting quickly usually limits the damage, and banks have clear processes for disputing payments you did not make.

takeaway: Urgency is the scammer's favourite tool: pause, verify through channels you found yourself, and check your transactions weekly.
